newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-WORLD SERIES COMES BACK TO YANKEE STADIUM.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-WORLD SERIES COMES BACK TO YANKEE STADIUM.

text.p: The World Series is coming back to Yankee Stadium, America's most storied sports venue and the centre stage of its national pastime.
Major League Baseball's championship series returns to New York on Saturday after a 15-year absence, but the memories of heroes, championships and a dab of pine tar never left.

The Yankees have been in 34 of the 91 World Series played, winning 23 of them. No one else is close. The team won five Series in a row from 1949-53, four in a row from 1936-39 and two in a row three times.
Yankees have won 20 of the 75 American League Most Valuable Player awards but only one Yankee star had a stadium built for him.
Babe Ruth was larger than life, and his triple-decker edifice was the grandest of its day. The Sultan of Swat broke it in with a grand slam on Opening Day, 1923.

It was in 1927 that he hit a historic 60 homers, a single-season record that lasted 34 years. The 60th was a one-bounder to the short right-field porch which nowadays would not be a legal four-bagger.

Ravaged by cancer, he said farewell on an emotional Babe Ruth Day on June 13, 1948, but it was Lou Gehrig, the teammate he was always uneasily paired with, who provided the stadium's most poignant moment and most famous speech in American sports.

On July 4, 1939, Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day, the Yankee first baseman, dying of the disease that would later bear his name, told teary-eyed fans: "Today I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth."
It was only two months after he had finally ended his record 14-year, 2,130-game playing streak. The Iron Horse and Pride of the Yankees died two years later at 37.
Joe DiMaggio was the next Yankee to define an era, and not just because he married sex goddess Marilyn Monroe.

On May 15, 1945, the Yankee Clipper got a single at the Stadium, a hit now noted only because it started a 56-game hitting streak that is one of the most astounding feats in baseball. The streak ended in Cleveland.

The son of an immigrant fisherman epitomised elegance, and his only display of emotion was a famous, frustrated kick in the dirt after Al Gionfriddo stole a home run from him here in the 1947 World Series.
In 1951 DiMaggio retired -- as a kid from Oklahoma named Mickey Mantle came on.
But the handover was far from smooth. Many blamed DiMaggio in centre for not warning Mantle in right about a drainage pipe during the '51 Series, and Mantle suffered the first of many injuries.

But he still could hit the ball a mile. There was his third-deck job that ended Game 3 of the 1964 Series, and the blast in 1963 that would have gone, an engineer estimated, 620 feet if the third-deck facade had not intervened 109 feet above the field. No one has ever hit one out of Yankee Stadium.

Teammate Roger Maris became the only man to surpass Ruth's 60 homers in 1961, year of the league's first expansion since 1901. By official decree, Maris's record was listed with an asterisk because he had eight more games to do it than Ruth.
Don Larsen achieved perfection in Game 5 of the 1956 World Series against the Brooklyn Dodgers, the only perfect game ever tossed in a World Series.
The right-hander used a no-windup delivery to set down the minimum 27 batters in a row, and the image of catcher Yogi Berra throwing himself into Larsen's arms is indelible in baseball memory.

In 1976, Chris Chambliss homered in the bottom of the ninth of Game 5 of the American League Championship Series, then fought his way through the fans to touch home plate and put the Yankees in the World Series for the first time in 12 years. The next year, they would win for the first time in 15.
George Steinbrenner, boss of baseball's richest club, was upping the ante. Among his best investments: Reggie Jackson.

Jackson put the seal to his "Mr October" nickname in Game 6 of the 1977 World Series when he hit three successive first-pitch home runs in a dramatic display not only of batting power but mesmerising will.
What is less remembered is he also homered on four successive swings, since he had smacked one in Game 5, then walked on four pitches before his trifecta.
Ruth also had three homers in a Series game, but not on successive pitches -- not in 1926, and not in 1928 when he did it again.
In 1978, Ron Guidry, known as "Louisiana Lightning," threw harder than seemed possible with his slight frame, and had a 25-3 year with a 1.74 ERA to lead the Yanks to a second championship in a row.
They have not won since, and have not reached the Series since 1981, but there was still plenty going on at the Stadium.

On July 24, 1983, Royals star George Brett hit a two-run homer off Goose Gossage with two out in the top of the ninth. But Yankee manager Billy Martin protested that the pine tar on Brett's bat exceeded the 18-inch limit on how high up the bat the substance could go, and the umpires agreed.

Few have forgotten the sight of Brett raging out of control when the umpires said his homer was an out. That decision was later reversed and a month later the game was played out from the point of the homer.

The New Yorkers had better luck with a ruling during last week's league championship series after 12-year-old fan Jeff Maier gloved Gary Jeter's eighth-inning fly ball out of the field of play and into the stands.
The Baltimore Orioles protested that the tying home run in a game the Yanks later won in the 11th should be disallowed and the game should be replayed from that point.
The protest was disallowed, and the 12-year-old "angel in the outfield" joined Yankee Stadium's gallery of memories.
